subject: How do we compare models after updating for error terms?

messages.author: 5b55811f2e3aab0a
messages.subject: How do we compare models after updating for error terms?
parts:
Hi all,

I am rerunning analyses with updated geomorph package in which 'anova.lm.rrpp' has replaced the 'nested.update' and 'advanced.procD.lm' functions for error term corrections and pairwise comparisons.

However I have a scenario that I'm not sure how to deal with in this case, as follows:.

 Let's say I'm  comparing models, and I specify my two models (e.g. null and full) using the anova() function which only accepts procD.lm objects. 

This is all good and well if the default error terms identified by geomorph are appropriate. However, if we decide that the default error terms are not appropriate, and we run the error term correction using anova(f1, error=c(...)), how can we compare models after such a correction? 

I tried assigning the error updated full and null models to objects and comparing them using anova() as follows:

null.model<-anova(f1, error=c(...))
full.model<-anova(f2, error=c(...))
anova(null.model, full.model)

However, this throws up the following error:
Error in UseMethod("anova") :
no applicable method for 'anova' applied to an object of class "anova.lm.rrpp"

Can this actually be done some other way? 

I always just assumed that because model comparisons are relative, it wouldn't matter if the models were updated for error terms or not. But looking at the differences in the F values in some models before and after updating with error=c(...), makes me rethink my logic.

Can you suggest any options for achieving both error term update and subsequent comaprison of updated models, rather than the default ones?

Thanks in advance for your advice. Really appreciate the community service the geomorph team are providing through this forum!

Regards,

Daniel

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] How do we compare models after updating for error terms?
parts:
Daniel,

 

You need to provide the anova function fitted models, not anovas of fitted models. Example:

 

library(RRPP)

data("PupfishHeads")

 

fit <- lm.rrpp(log(headSize) ~ sex, data = PupfishHeads)

fit2 <- lm.rrpp(log(headSize) ~ sex + locality, data = PupfishHeads)

anova(fit, fit2)

 

Dean

parts:
Hi Dean, 

Yes, of course! How silly of me...

I did try this with the fitted shape variables and got a curious result.... so the fitted shape variables are presumably $Y of the full model - fit.full4 as specified below). The 4 models I'm interested in comparing are:

fit.null4<-lm.rrpp(smeltshp.lm.full$Y~sex+logcs, iter=999, RRPP=T)
fit.hab4<-lm.rrpp(smeltshp.lm.full$Y~habitat*sex+logcs, iter=999, RRPP=T)
fit.loc4<-lm.rrpp(smeltshp.lm.full$Y~location*sex+logcs, iter=999, RRPP=T)
fit.full4<-lm.rrpp(smeltshp.lm.full$Y~(habitat/location)*sex+logcs,iter=999, RRPP=T)
anova(fit.null4, fit.hab4, fit.loc4, fit.full4)

In this case, habitat (i.e. river or reservoir or lotic vs lentic) is the primary factor of interest.

I then got the following result from the ANOVA model comparison as you suggested above:

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals Number of permutations: 1000 Estimation method: Ordinary Least Squares Effect sizes (Z) based on F distributions ResDf Df RSS SS MS Rsq F Z P Pr(>F) smeltshp.lm.full$Y ~ sex + logcs (Null) 666 1 0.55757 0.000000 smeltshp.lm.full$Y ~ habitat * sex + logcs 664 2 0.53146 0.026116 0.0130578 0.045289 16.314 9.4658 0.001 smeltshp.lm.full$Y ~ location * sex + logcs 646 20 0.38148 0.176088 0.0088044 0.305365 14.909 14.6291 0.001 smeltshp.lm.full$Y ~ (habitat/location) * sex + logcs 646 20 0.38148 0.176088 0.0088044 0.305365 14.909 14.6291 0.001 Total 668 0.57665
Interestingly, the intermediate and full model have identical results. I suspect this is because the levels of location (i.e. each individual river or reservoir that was sampled for my target fish species - smelt), captures the same information about differences in body shape as designating each sampling location as either river or reservoir.

In other words, the result will be the same if I am comparing the individuals from the 5 indiviual river and 5 reservoir groups, or lumped them together and compared fish from one of two groups - i.e. based on their membership of river / reservoir 

Also,  for completeness, I looked at pairwise differences and this indicated that location appeared to be more important than habitat, but because groups did not differ by flow habitat (i.e. river vs reservoir fish). More often there were actually differences within habitat types. And in fact, sex had to do with this, but very little. 

hume.f:georges.m 0.031542495 0.04290123 -1.267798313 0.894 # Fish from Hume reservoir and Georges River were not significantly different in shape.
hume.f:hume.m 0.015049061 0.01303636 2.677253148 0.003 # Female and male fish within Hume reservoir were significantly different in shape.
hume.m:nillahcoot.m 0.022649343 0.02185722 1.951045137 0.025 # Hume and Nillahcootie reservoirs - male body shape is significantly different between them.

kiewa.m:ovens.m 0.029661506 0.02953508 1.669318554 0.047 # Two river populations - male body shape is again significantly different
lake nep.m:nillahcoot.m 0.026401798 0.02484764 2.204862245 0.015 # Two resevoir populations - males only different
nillahcoot.m:ovens.m 0.030902308 0.03088791 1.649886297 0.050 # The only reservoir group (Nillahcootie males) that differs from a river group (Ovens males)

Do you think the above is a feasible explanation for the lack of difference in fit.loc4 and fit.full.4? If so, I suspect it's probably worth tossing both the original alternative hypothesis that body shape is different between habitats, and based on the post-hoc/pairwise analysis, that body shape differences are repeatable among any at all.

Or do you see something else that could be happening here?

Thanks again for the advice, really appreciate it.

Regards,

Daniel

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] How do we compare models after updating for error terms?
parts: Daniel, I think you answered your own question. If your sampling has individuals that are largely overlapping for river and reservoir, one cannot expect differentiation of models when using one or the other. In this case, the sampling design has created multicollinearity of several independent variables; making them highly associated.

Dean
